newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Netcare defends union role in Clinics buy.
newsitem.headline: Netcare defends union role in Clinics buy.

text.p: Network Healthcare Holdings Ltd (Netcare) on Wednesday defended labour federation Cosatu's financial role in its acquisition of Clinic Holdings Ltd (Clinics).
The left-wing Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) had been accused in the press of going against its own principles by investing in the private health care sector.
But Gil Mahlati of black empowerment group Dingaka, representing black medics, said the belief that Cosatu wanted to nationalise health care was incorrect.

"Cosatu wants a national health care system which is driven nationally," Mahlati told an analysts' presentation on Wednesday, adding that within that system government could purchase services from the private sector.

Netcare announced at the weekend that it had bought Clinics for 920 million rand, making it the biggest managed health care group in South Africa with 5,550 beds and a market share about 50 percent more than its nearest competitor.
Cosatu's investment arm and three of its unions together with Dingaka will own about 28 percent of Netcare, following the transaction.
Netcare chief executive officer Jack Shevel said the inclusion of black partners would also help in securing government contracts.
Netcare has traded successfully since its listing in December with the share more than doubling its price in four months. The company is ungeared and has cash resources worth 25 million rand.
It reported earnings for the half year ended February up 3.8 cents from a loss of 7.3 cents for the proforma year ended August 31, 1996.
Clinics last month reported a first half loss of 7.66 million rand from a previous profit of 21.02 million rand for the six months ended March 31.
The forecast earnings per share for the year ended September 1998 is 34.7 cents for Clinics and 16.6 cents for Netcare.
Shevel said the decline in profits in Clinics would be arrested through the substantial reduction of Clinics' interest-bearing debt and a change in management control from August 8.

The increased use of facilities and rationalisation opportunities which existed within the combined group would also help stop declining earnings at Clinics and put it on a path to achieve forecast earnings for the year ending September 1998.

The price for Clinics was fair since replicating the same infrastruture including staff would not be achieved at the same price even if the government moratorium on new clinic licences was not in place, Shevel said.
"Combining Netcare and Clinic Holdings enables us to acquire an enormously valuable infrastructure within Clinic Holdings, which enhances our critical mass and geographical spread," Shevel said.
